title: When blame becomes the culture
author: Dr Haili Hughes
summary: Hughes opens with the story of a colleague blamed for mishandling a task he was never properly inducted into, using it to illustrate how blame in schools and trusts rarely announces itself - it arrives dressed as 'concern', 'quality assurance' or 'just flagging'. Drawing on Amy Edmondson's work on psychological safety, she argues that accountability language can be corrupted into a hunt for someone to hold responsible, teaching staff to hide problems rather than surface them, which is fatal in the uncertain, interdependent work of school improvement. She also draws on the Church of England's National Society work on 'flourishing' and Samuel Crome's writing on team performance to argue blame individualises failure that is often systemic, and offers leaders a set of reframed questions ('what made this more likely?' instead of 'who allowed this to happen?') as a practical alternative.
points: Hughes's central image - blame arriving 'dressed as concern... quality assurance... just flagging' - names a subtle leadership failure mode that looks professional while corroding trust.
She invokes Edmondson's psychological safety research to argue that a blame culture doesn't just feel unpleasant; it structurally breaks the feedback loops schools need to learn and improve.
Her critique of the 'heroic leader myth' in multi-academy trusts - where success is attributed to the model and failure to the school - names a specific structural driver of blame culture.
Her reframed questions ('what made this more likely?' rather than 'who allowed this to happen?') give leaders a concrete, transferable diagnostic tool for replacing blame with useful inquiry.
quotes: This is how blame often works in schools and trusts. It rarely announces itself as blame. It arrives as concern. As quality assurance. As just flagging. The language stays professional, but the effect is corrosive.
Edmondson is explicit that managing through fear no longer works in uncertain, interdependent work. In my opinion schools are the very definition of uncertain and interdependent places.
A blame culture is not merely unpleasant. It is anti-flourishing. It asks adults to model courage for pupils while punishing candour among staff.
In a blame culture, a poor set of Year 11 outcomes becomes a problem with the Head of Department. Each label may contain some truth, but the framing is narrow and often unfair.
Instead of Who allowed this to happen? try What made this more likely? Instead of Why wasn't this done? try What got in the way? This is not softness. In fact, it is often more rigorous.
